utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. On this Tuesday, 29th of May, 2007, would I like to greet all the parties, the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, the accused, as well as all the other people present in this courtroom, but I would first like to hand the floor to the registrar for some IC numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. 1D has submitted a response to the OTP objections regarding 1D exhibits tendered through Witness BC, and this list shall be given Exhibit number IC 580 under seal. Several parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Philip Watkins. The list submitted by the OTP shall be given Exhibit number IC 581 under seal. The list submitted by 1D shall be given Exhibit number IC 582 under seal. The list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit number IC 583. The list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit number IC 584 under seal. The list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit number IC 585 under seal. That's everything for now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Scott, last week we noticed on the intranet site of the Tribunal the mention to the effect that a commission for disappeared people in Bosnia would have found 16 bodies out of which 13 would belong to BiH soldiers, by people -- soldiers that had disappeared on the 9th of May, 1993 in Mostar. The press agency indicated that those 13 people were identified through -- through rings and watches that were on them. At this point, can you tell me if the Prosecution knew of this or was aware of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, and all those in the courtroom. Your Honour, I'm afraid I must say that we were not aware of it other than through news accounts ourselves. I think we had heard of it before it came on the internet, but it was also through -- it was also indirectly. So I don't want to stand up and say that the OTP had had some sort of inside track on this some weeks and weeks ago. I think we heard about it last week. Your Honour, I think it's fair to say that the Prosecution for years has tried to locate these particular -- what we suspect to be the bodies of these people who went missing, and there's been a huge effort by both the ICTY and, I think, local authorities to do that, and all the leads previously have not come to anything. It does appear from this information, just in general terms, it's quite possible that there could be the connection to the 13 people who went missing from the Vranica building and then later found in the mechanical faculty building, but we already started inquiries for more specific information and that's already been put into motion since last week, and I will report further to the Chamber, if the Court desires, when we have more information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The second topic is the question regarding the witness that is about to testify. Last week we've indicated that the Prosecution would have five hours and the Defence six hours, and then we noticed at the last minute in fact that there was going to be a witness that was going to be called back on Thursday. So the witness that is going to be called back will testify during two days, today and tomorrow, and the SLO informed you by e-mail of this last week. We learnt, and I thank the Prosecution, that they wanted to raise a topic with this witness, a topic that was not in the written statement of this witness, the destruction of the Old Bridge in Mostar, and the Judges that evoked this question deem that this is a topic that is interesting to raise through this witness, so the questions will only -- the questions will only talk about his written statement [as interpreted]. I also believe that Mr. Kovacic wanted to intervene. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom, and particularly the Trial Chamber. Your Honour, you have already in fact said something that I was about to raise. What I wanted to do was to remind you, as you've just said, that on the 24th of May the Trial Chamber gave us the amount of time we would roughly have for the incoming witness, that is to say five hours for the Prosecution and six hours for the Defence. However, later on, as you yourself already said, there was some changes, and an additional witness was interpolated for one day, and then in the e-mail towards the end of the week you recalculated the time. Now, Your Honour, you have given us an explanation for that revised decision by which you have reduced our time for the cross-examination; however, in the meantime this morning there was another change that took place because the Prosecution, as things now stand, informed the Defence teams and the Trial Chamber that the witness will be heard under Rule 92 ter. And to all intents and purposes, in view of the fact that the Prosecution retains the right for examination, I think that this is making unlawful use of 92 ter, because from the point of view of the Defence, of course, according to this calculation, that is say three hours for the cross-examination and for the six accused, they have as much time as the Prosecution does, so that the time they put in the statement, they will have time to present the statement and additional time to examine the witness. Now, I'd like to remind you of a previous ruling whereby you gave instructions to the Prosecution about how to go about examining and dealing with witnesses under Rule 62 ter -- 92 ter, and when a statement is being introduced you said that all we need to do is to verify and see if the witness actually gave the statement and signed it, and the Prosecution might have a little time to present certain documents along with the statement. Now, in its letter, the Prosecution has told us that they have an additional plan afoot. That is to say they will be examining the witness directly. They will have an examination-in-chief of the witness, which means that they will use two mechanisms, the 92 ter for introducing the statement, but also examination-in-chief of the witness as well. So they're going to benefit from those two mechanisms. Now, I consider that that is reason of -- or, rather, that the reasoning in Rule 92 ter -- the reasoning behind it is to enable each party to introduce the statement previously given, but it certainly is not -- the reasoning behind that provision is certainly not to allow for both things to take place, that is to say a statement which apropos has hearsay evidence and direct testimony as well, because the reasonable behind 92 ter was to precisely allow the opposite side, in this case the Defence, to challenge those assertions and allegations made in the statement. So in actual fact, the Defence finds itself in a position where it will have to refute and challenge four categories of proof and evidence which we're going to deal with through this witness, the first category being one that we would have to test during cross-examination because it contains elements from a previously given statement which the Prosecution means to introduce through Rule 92 ter. The other category is the witness testimony, live testimony in court, and we heard that there will be three hours of live testimony, and the third category is the documents which the Prosecution will be using when examining the witness, and they will be tendering those documents into evidence ultimately, and the fourth category comprises the documents which either the witness himself has prepared or other members of the same institution have prepared and dealing with the same events in the same period of time, and the Prosecution did not intend to use those documents. So I consider that in conformity with the standard of proceedings for the Defence, these are very closely defined four categories which we challenge, and it is my proposal in the end that once you hear - because I'm just guessing at the moment - but once we have heard the witness and once we have seen which documents the Prosecution wishes to present and tender or, rather, those they do not wish to present and tender, that you have a rethink and reassessment of the time afterwards and decide whether the Defence teams might need more time accorded to them. Now, I fully understand that we have reached a point -- or, rather, that we were under time constraints, all of us together, after we found out that on Thursday we would be having another witness coming in, in the meantime, but as has been the case on previous occasions at times, I see no reason that if we feel after hearing the testimony that if this is necessary that we accord additional time to the Defence at some point in future. And I'd like to mention that perhaps the positive element in all this is that this testimony -- that this witness resides in the Netherlands and he works in The Hague, so that does not mean any additional difficulties in terms of travel arrangements and so on because the witness is in fact here. And one more fact that I'd like to mention is this, for us all to have the same picture: I think, Your Honours, saw the statement of before 1992 which the Prosecution wishes to tender under Rule 92 ter. I'd just like to remind you that a significant portion of that statement relates to the events in Gornji Vakuf at the time when Gornji Vakuf is not in the indictment. So in my opinion it is a totally irrelevant portion of the statement, and therefore I'm asking whether it merits being introduced under 92 ter, Rule 92 ter. And also, the statement deals in part with the events in Bugojno. Bugojno is not in the indictment at all. It doesn't figure there at all. And so the question arises whether the Trial Chamber will allow just the partial admission of a statement because most of it is irrelevant. That's the first point. And secondly, we don't have an instrument by which to portions of the statement; there is no Rule governing that issue So even if you allow it in under Rule 92 ter, you must specify which portion -- I don't think that would be possible. You wouldn't be able to say which portion is admitted and which isn't because that would go against the grain of the logics of the statement, as it was recorded and as given by the witness. And now finally, my question is this: After we see exactly what the Prosecution wishes to accomplish today, and for illustration purposes let me just say that this morning we received from the Prosecution six or seven documents which were disclosed previously, I think on the 10th of May unless I'm very much mistaken, but which were not translated. Of that number, only one or two were in Dutch, in fact. But anyway, we weren't -- had not had time to have them shown to our client in B/C/S. So that is another obstacle. And I'd like to conclude with this proposal: Once we hear the examination of the witness, I should like to ask the Trial Chamber to decide and see whether the Defence does indeed need additional time so that it would be proportionate to what the Prosecutor is introducing either through Rule 92 ter or through the examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your proposition, which is written on line 10, page 6, is precisely what the Chamber was going to take into account, but I will hand the floor to Mr. Scott for a brief answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, I have to observe that it seems that we're -- a great effort is being made to create more problems rather than less. Rule 92 ter was created very -- for very clear purposes, and that was to allow evidence to be taken more efficiently, and the point of Rule 92 ter is to take evidence more efficiently in less time, not more time, and yet the impression I have from some of the comments by Mr. Kovacic and others is that somehow the use of 92 ter actually expands or makes things more difficult, and I think quite the contrary. The Rule quite plainly provides, as we've discussed before, the use of the Rule in whole or in part. Now, what does that mean? The Prosecution submits and this has been the Prosecution practice in other Chambers and other Chambers have followed this practice and we would ask this Chamber to follow the same practice, is that -- and in particular at this stage of the trial. The Chamber has heard a great deal of evidence on some -- on various parts of the case. Let's say Mostar, for example. A witness comes in and let's just choose a round number of something like 60 paragraphs of a statement. Most of those statement -- most of the paragraphs deal with what we've come to call the crime base, perhaps in Mostar. Now, the Prosecution does not want to forego that evidence. It would like to and believes that that evidence should be received into the record, but at the same time does not see any particular point in taking precious courtroom time or the Judges' time to go through all that evidence viva voce, which could take another couple of hours. 92 ter is specifically, in part, a response to that exact situation, whereby the Prosecution can stand up -- the witness comes into the courtroom. The statement can be put in. Those parts -- most of the statement can be -- most of the evidence can be taken by way of statement, and then precious courtroom time can be dedicated to only those most important parts, perhaps the new parts, or the most important parts, a meeting with one of the accused, a conversation with one of the accused, and we take that time and focus on that and then also address documents and exhibits that go with that witness. Now, I don't know. For some reason that seems eminently reasonable to me and what the Rule contemplated, and was clearly what the Rule contemplated at the time that rules committee considered, at which I was present. So I don't understand the-- all the problems, quite frankly. The Chamber well knows, and it's no secret, that the time and -- for the remainder of the Prosecution case is limited, and we would propose that this Rule should be used more rather than less and that witnesses can come in, some of their evidence can be submitted in writing. Other parts of their evidence can be the focus of more courtroom discussion, as other Chambers have done that. I know it was used extensively in the Krajisnik case that way I know it's been used in the Milutinovic case in that way to good effect. So I don't see any reason why the problems in this particular courtroom or Chamber should be different than the successful use of the Rule in other cases and Chambers. The bottom line, Your Honour, is that the total amount of time taken would be less not more. This witness was scheduled to be a five-hour witness. If we can do it now through 92 ter and otherwise as a three-hour witness then I don't understand what the complaint is. We have reduced the total amount of time to take the witness. That seems to me like a benefit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Scott. Thank you very much to use this article, state this article and use it very -- or very useful Rule, rather. The Defence will also be able to use the same procedure. We've already indicated that the Prosecution -- that the Prosecutor may ask additional questions under Rule 92 ter, and I believe that the Prosecutor wishes to use all the documents that are presented to put questions on these documents, and I believe that in fact the written statement is an advantage because it saves us time. And as you know, the Chamber may admit as a whole or in part documents, and if the Defence believes in the end that some portions should be withdrawn, the Defence can always ask the withdrawal of some passages, portions, portions that, for instance, do not appear in the indictment. You've stated Gornji Vakuf and Bugojno. So furthermore, at this stage we have decided that the accusation -- the Prosecution will have three hours, the Defence will in turn also have three hours, one hour which will be given to Mr. Praljak and 25 minutes for each counsel or each accused. As Mr. Kovacic stated, if after the examination-in-chief we realise that additional time should be granted, we will inform you of this and then we will give you additional time. Of course, this will all depend on documents since we do not know what will come out of the questions put to the witness. We will see things better when we end the examination-in-chief, but for now we will grant the Prosecution the three hours already indicated, and if additional time is needed, it is, of course, possible to call the witness back, as you've indicated yourself, Mr. Kovacic, because he is not too far away. Very well. Now I will ask the usher to bring the witness in since we've already spent 25 minutes. Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, could I just say something because the practice in the Krajisnik case was mentioned and I do still retain some recollection of that matter. It's true, of course, that 92 bis was used quite extensively, as it was bound to be in a case of that size, but, actually, the particular technique that was used as the case developed for time saving was the use of Rule 89(F) in a slightly different way, which was to take a witness fairly quickly through matters which were in a written statement or perhaps just to introduce very quickly certain elements of a witness's statement -- evidence that were in the written statement to save time and short circuit that and get very quickly to the heart of the matters where the Defence could reasonably ask that the matter should be led conventionally as far as possible without leading questions. That did save a lot of time, but it leads to this, which ties in with what we understand to have been the central point in Mr. Kovacic's submissions just now, which is that it is then very unfair and artificial if one doesn't allow for the fact that the evidence which has been adduced in that way very quickly by means of Rule 89(F) is in substance the equivalent of what might have been quite extensively oral examination-in-chief so that a corresponding and satisfactory allowances made in the time for the Defence in cross-examination, otherwise it works very unfairly. And there was more than one point in Mr. Kovacic's submissions, but a central point in his submissions, which we endorse and which is entirely sensible, and Your Honours did apparently have that in mind, so we don't really understand why the Prosecution are so upset about it, is that what when we get to the point of seeing how this combination of different techniques of presenting evidence has worked for that particular witness, the Court will assess as apparently you're going to do what is required and we frankly don't see anything objectionable about that. It makes completes sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much, Mr. Stewart. Let's call the witness in. Thank you for reminding us of the Krajisnik -- of the way Article 89 -- Rule 89(F) was used in the Krajisnik case, which still, of course, exists notwithstanding Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. I would like to check if you hear me. If that's the case, could you please tell me if you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like you to stand up because I will ask you to read a solemn declaration. Could you please give us your full name and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am Rudy Gerritsen. My date of birth is the 9th of May, 1954.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell us what is your current rank in the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Have you ever testified before an international tribunal regarding events which took place in the former Yugoslavia, and, if that's the case, in which case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I testified two times before and -- in two cases, and the names I haven't in my memory at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But you've testified it in a case because I recognise it was in the case Hadzihasanovic and Kubura. I would like to ask you to read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. You may sit down, Colonel. Let me explain to you the procedure before this hearing begins, this hearing in which you are called as a witness. You are going to be answering questions put to you by the Prosecutor. You must have met him during the weekend or at least this morning. The Prosecutor will show you documents which he probably mentioned during the proofing session, and after that the Defence counsel, as well as the accused, will put questions to you. The four Judges before you will also be able to intervene at any point to put questions to you, but since not long ago we prefer to intervene at the very end unless it is -- there is a point that we would like to raise that's extremely important or a point regarding documents. And if you need to take a break for any reason, personal reasons, please let us know. Since you've testified already, you know how these things go. This is your third time. And as you know, we take breaks every 90 minutes. So without further ado, I shall ask the Prosecution to give a brief summary under Article 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon to Your Honours and to everybody else in and around the courtroom. I would begin with the 65 ter summary, and I'd like to emphasise for Your Honours and for my colleagues on the Defence that this summary is prepared and is confined to issues linked to the indictment and none other. In this case the witness served as an ECMM monitor in Gornji Vakuf between the 18th of July, 1993, and the 15th of September, 1993. Within the AOR there were two local commanders in Bugojno and Gornji Vakuf and they were subordinate to the operational zone commander who was Zeljko Siljeg, whose headquarters were in a factory in Prozor. There was also a unit of military police based in Prozor. The witness felt that Zeljko Siljeg had no authority Croatian Defence Council military police in Prozor. The witness felt that Zeljko Siljeg was always well-informed because he was never surprised when told about things happening within his AOR. On the 31st of July, 1993, ECMM members were requested to go to the Croatian Defence Council headquarters in Prozor. Zeljko Siljeg introduced the witness to General Slobodan Praljak, and introduced him as the overall commander of the Croatian Defence Council troops in Bosnia. It was clear by his manner that he was Zeljko Siljeg's superior. Slobodan Praljak said that the main focus of the Croatian Defence Council would be a cease-fire. There would be freedom of movement for UNPROFOR. He wanted to know what the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina thought of the Geneva peace talks. On the 11th of August, 1993, ECMM representatives talked to the chairman of the humanitarian committee in Prozor, Ljubica Beljo, regarding the Muslim population from Prozor that had been put into one place. On the 16th of August, 1993, the mayor of Prozor, Mijo Jozic, told them that the Muslims had been gathered in one place for their own safety. Later on, on the 19th of August, Zeljko Siljeg gave them permission to visit Muslims detained in the school in Prozor. The inmates were not POWs. The witness thought that this was part of ethnic -- an ethnic cleansing campaign of the Croats. ECMM representatives managed to talk to some detainees and were told that they were being used for forced label to dig trenches on the front line in Gornji Vakuf. They said that beatings had been occurred in the school but when the new commander arrived the beatings had decreased. 400 Muslim men aged between 16 and 60 years had been transported to other detention camps in Capljina and Ljubuski. The guards were Croatian Defence Council soldiers and not military police. They also visited the area of Podgrad. There was only one road into this area --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters who don't have the text. Thank you. Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Sorry. There was only one road into this area which had a barrier on the road entrance. They were told that there were some 1.700 Muslims living there with 30 to 70 in each house. They said that they had only flour to eat. The witness was told by a woman that she was raped by Mario Dolic. They were also told that Croatian Defence Council soldiers would come at night and rape the women. There were only women, children, and elderly men in the area. On the 20th of August, 1993, the witness went to the village of Duge. There were 700 to 800 people living there, 20 to 30 in each house. These people came from Prozor and surroundings and had nowhere to go. Their men had been taken away. On the 1st of September, 1993, the witness met with Zeljko Siljeg and asked him about the movement of Muslims that had occurred. He said that he knew that they had been moved to Muslim territory but it was an operation by the military police and that they had acted independently of the Croatian Defence Council. The witness thinks that it was a deliberate and planned ethnic cleansing of Muslims from Prozor. That concludes the 65 ter statement, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Colonel Gerritsen, good afternoon. Did you ever provide a written statement to the investigators of the ICTY regarding the I just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you give this statement on the 9th of April [sic] 2002?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And at the time you provided this written statement, did you answer the questions of the investigator truthfully?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you answer the questions freely and without any form of coercion?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And was that interview conducted in English?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: In English.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And at the conclusion of the interview, was your statement read back to you?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you then sign and initial that statement in the English language?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: At this point, Your Honours, could I ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit number 10030, with the ERN number 02192545 to 3556.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Colonel, could you turn to the first document on this booklet that's been handed to you under tab reference 10030.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Is this the statement which you gave to the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: This is the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And is that your signature on the document and are those your initials on each page of the statement?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And when you travelled here to The Hague a few days ago I think yesterday you met with myself and an investigator. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And at that time you were given an opportunity to review the statement. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And I think upon reviewing the statement you had some very few additions or corrections to make to the statement. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Is it true to say that you had one correction and one addition in total?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And I think -- and the Prosecution has notified the Defence of this, i think that as far as the only correction that you wanted to make was on page 8, paragraph 7, instead of the use of the word "concentration camp" you wanted that changed to "ghetto."

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And in addition during the course of proofing, you added to your statement the fact that you -- when you had met General Praljak in Prozor on the 31st of July, 1993, that the discussion turned to the subject of Mostar and the bridge in Mostar, and that General Praljak made certain comments about that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And do you stand over everything you said in your statement and your amended statement, and if you were to give the evidence again today de novo from the start, would you say everything you have said in the statement?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, for the -- for the record is it a correct -- I think it's indicated on page 1 of your statement that you are a member of the ECMM and you arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina in July of 1993?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And we see from the statement that you were assigned to the area of Gornji Vakuf and that your period of duty began on the 18th of July, 1993. Can you tell when it came to an end?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: The 15th of September at Gornji Vakuf. I went to Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And just for the record, could you tell us, when using the name Gornji Vakuf what was that area of responsibility what towns, village -- what towns did that include?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: It includes Prozor and Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And when you arrived from -- from Croatia you went to Zenica. Did you have a briefing in Zenica before arriving in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I had, from Jean-Pierre Thebault, and my colleague monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity of examining previous reports and articles concerning your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, you were assigned to Gornji Vakuf. What did you understand your role as monitor to entail, just for the record?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: We made daily reports and within several headlines. Each daily report was the same from the headlines concerning the military paragraph and assessment, humanitarian, and several other -- others.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And that will be part of your duties, but in terms your role as a monitor, what did you understand that to be?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: To monitor. And that's important to understand. We were not investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And in the course of monitoring, would this involve meeting various actors within your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. We met several kind of men and women, priest, Imams, military commanders, majors from the villages and towns, and normal people.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And before we come to that, just going back to when you arrived in Gornji Vakuf, is it correct to say that the other team members working from Gornji Vakuf were a gentleman by the name of Skat-Rordam and there was also a Mr. Peter Hauenstein?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, Skat-Rordam from the Danish army; Peter Hauenstein, Canadian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: You mention the reporting. To whom did you make these reports?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: We sent these reports through Capsat, a satellite medium, through Zenica, and from Zenica they made a total report from all team members and they send it to Zagreb. From there to the capitals of Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you prepare these reports working alone or were you working in tandem with your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Together with my colleagues. Most of the times when I -- most of the time I worked with Peter Hauenstein. He was a Canadian, and he -- his English, of course, was very well, and he -- he wrote the biggest part of these statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And if you didn't actually write the report per se, would you -- would you in all situations be familiar with its contents before it was dispatched to the regional centre?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I was always familiar. We always discussed what should be in the reports. I also wrote some paragraphs mostly every day. The only thing he did was to correct my English.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, the Trial Chamber will have seen examples of -- of ECMM reports over the last number of weeks and months, but just so that we're on the one page and we know what we're talking about the same document, I wonder, would you turn to Exhibit number 9653. Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I have that in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And the top of the page is dated the 18th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And can I ask you, is this an example of what your daily report would look like?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That is example. The first daily report I have written together with Captain Ron [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And if you look at the headings, it says it's from V2 Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Is V2 is a code word for your team?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: It's a code word for my team, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And it went to CC Travnik?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: CC Travnik, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And if we look at, for example, paragraph 3, military activity, where it says, "Today an UNFOR patrol was denied passage into Pajic Polje until UNPROFOR could -- would escort some Croat casualties." Is this the type of information that you gathered on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And on what basis would you draft these reports? What or who were your principal sources of information?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That was our own monitoring. That's the most important part, what we saw by ourselves. And the other part is information from BritBat, also located in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you ever have the opportunity of seeing written reports from BritBat?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No. We always went to the operation room from BritBat and there we gathered our information and we got the information from discussion with Graham Binns, a company commander of the Prince of Wales Own Regiment of Yorkshire.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And once the report had been sent to Travnik, where would it go from there?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: To Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And what would Zenica do with it?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Make an overall overview from the several reports which came to Zenica. For instance -- for example, Tuzla also sent their report to Zenica, and it was all put together in -- in a shorter way and then sent to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And would a copy of that be sent to -- to your AOR so you would be aware of what was going in other AORs?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Could you just for the record turn to Exhibit 9654.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And it's a document dated the 21 of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: July, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And it's from RC Zenica to HQ Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: And all team members.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: With copies to all team members. Is this the type of roll-up report that you're referring?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: This is the type, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And if you turn to the second page, for example, it talks about CC Travnik, Zenica, the situation in Gornji Vakuf is still tense. Heavy fighting is going on around Bugojno, where BiH seems to gain terrain. Would this have been information you would have supplied to them?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And if you go back to the first page, I'm just wondering, under paragraph 2, it's not your area, it's CC Mostar area, but there on the second paragraph it makes a reference to exchange of prisoners, and I'm wondering was this an issue which you dealt with within your AOR, the exchange of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: We dealt with exchange not in my time I was in Gornji Vakuf. We didn't have had an exchange of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you attempt --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Exchange of prisoners we had, yes. I -- yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: It was always one way, not an -- an exchange at the same moment. We had an exchange at the same moment with casualties but not at the same moment with prisoners. It was always one way.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And do you know who within the HVO, who within the hierarchy of the HVO would have had overall or ultimate responsibility in terms of the exchange of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: The operational zone command Siljeg and his superiors above him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And do you know anything about his superiors above him? Do you know who exactly would have been in charge?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, I met General Praljak, and at that time he was obviously the commander of Siljeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll come to that in a moment. Now, you've told us that Gornji Vakuf AOR included Prozor, Gornji Vakuf, and Bugojno. Were you given a detailed briefing or background information on arrival or prior to arrival by your colleagues as to what the situation was on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: He tried to do Skat-Rordam, his best but there was a lack of time because the first day I arrive the classes started in Bugojno. So later on I -- I would have -- show more, show more, but that came at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And just for the record, can you tell me what -- what the position was on the ground in Bugojno on your arrival?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I arrived on a Sunday. We got on Sunday meeting the message that the fighting started in Bugojno. Next day I -- I went to Bugojno and the fightings were going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And what was the position in Gornji Vakuf, briefly?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: ABiH was attacking and trying to -- conquering the city of Bugojno [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And what was the position in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: In Prozor, HVO was in command and at that time in Prozor there were no fightings.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, we were speaking a little earlier about what your -- what your duties why and what your role would involve. Would I be correct in saying that your daily routine would involve you meeting various individuals for the purpose of information gathering?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Were those individuals be both military and civilians?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think there seems to be a mistake in the transcript so perhaps we could clear that up straight away otherwise we won't be able to use it. In line 16, page 25, the question was [In English] [Previous translation continues] "... and what was the position in Gornji Vakuf, briefly." Then we have the answer, army of BiH was attacking and trying to conquer the city of Bugojno. So we don't know what we are talking about Gornji Vakuf or Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry for -- for this mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There is similar mistake 30 line above that. I didn't want to intervene but --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: It needs to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I come --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please have the witness specify what he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Just go back to Bugojno for a moment and could you just explain the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: In Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: In Bugojno BiH was attacking to conquer Bugojno with the aim to conquer Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And what was happening at the same time in the region of Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: In Gornji Vakuf there was also some fighting and shelling mostly on a daily -- on a daily basis from HVO to Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And farther south then if we move towards Prozor, was there any fighting going on there?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Most of the time not. That was only in the period I have been there for two months. One attack on tanks, two 54s from HBH [sic], and that's mainly it. And in the surroundings of Prozor the HBH attacked a village called Uzdol. That was the 15th of September. That was mainly it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, I was asking you, your daily routine would have involved you meeting with both military and civilian personages and personalities within your AOR; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And in paragraph 6 of your statement you mention Colonel Zeljko Siljeg, and you describe him as the operational zone commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And was he -- was he one of the principal HVO commanders within your AOR?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, how soon after did you actually start your duties of monitors? Did you start them immediately?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I started them immediately, the 19th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, I don't propose to focus on the events which occurred in Bugojno or in Gornji Vakuf, but would it be correct to say that the initial focus of your task was directed towards what was happening in Bugojno and Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And would it be correct to say that towards the end of July the battle, the fighting, was moving southwards?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Was moving southwards and my attention, and also from my colleague monitor, of course, was also drawn to Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And if we turn to Exhibit 92 -- 9626.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: It's a document dated the 29th of July, 1993. Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Is this a daily report for that date?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that -- that is the daily report signed by Hauenstein, Gerritsen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Are you one of the authors of this report?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, Gerritsen has signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And we see that the H positions -- the HV positions are -- still remain in Pajic Polje. Prozor continues to see a build-up of troops. UNPROFOR reports much movement of soldiers and equipment. S in paragraph 1?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: At the Makljen check-point there was a large amount of HVO troops moving to the north?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Was the Makljen check-point an elevated position situated between Prozor and Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, kind of in the middle of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So as the fighting was intensifying, do you remember, on the 31st of July, were you and your colleagues summoned to the HVO headquarters in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: The 31st of July, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And when you arrived there, who -- whom did you meet?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Siljeg and Praljak, General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did Colonel Siljeg introduce General Praljak to you?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And in what way did he introduce him to you?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: He introduce him to me as General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did he say what position he occupied?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. He was commander from the HVO. I do not exactly know. I think from the whole of troops in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Was he introduced -- did you understand from what he said that he was superior to Colonel Siljeg?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have really been tolerant, but the last four or five questions were evidently leading questions. They are the kind of questions used as examples of leading questions at seminars with our colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I disagree, Your Honour, because in the statement it's clearly indicated that this witness met with General Praljak, so I'm merely supplementing what's contained in the statement. This is not a witness who is giving evidence strictly viva voce. If it were viva voce I would certainly agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely irrelevant, Your Honour. This is absolutely irrelevant. If there is a statement, this still does not give the Prosecutor the right to put leading questions. Secondly, there is no need to put questions about things that are already in the statement. So I move that the Chamber instruct my learned friend to put questions according to the rules. In this case, they cannot be leading questions. And, Your Honours, I sat quietly through four or five such questions, but enough is enough, and if my colleague does not agree that it's a leading question, let him look at the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Flynn, you should not be asking leading questions, but I will note that at line 14, page 29, you asked what position General Praljak occupied. That's not a leading question. The witness said [In English] the HVO. [In French] Therefore, the witness has answered your question, and it's not a leading question. So please be very careful, Mr. Flynn. This is a 92 ter procedure. We already have received the written statement of the witness. Please only ask questions if they have an added value, so to speak. If it's not the case, don't put these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: In your -- in your statement you described a number of issues in general terms that you discussed with General Praljak. Can I ask you, did you raise with him any humanitarian concerns which you may have had concerning the treatment of prisoners --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Flynn, here again Mr. Kovacic could have stood up. In order to avoid any problems, you should have said the following: You dealt with a number of issues with Mr. Praljak. He would have answered yes. And then you ask what kind of issues, and then he says, well, for example, humanitarian issues. That's much easier that way. I know that you're trying to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I take note of that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And indeed my understanding of the 92 process was to supplement what the witness has said in his -- in his written statement and then to put documents with it to corroborate it. But I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can you tell it us what subjects were discussed during your meeting with General Praljak?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Humanitarian, political, and military subjects.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did the subject of war crimes and behaviour of troops on the field come up?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: They also came up.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: What other subjects did you raise with the general?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, we -- we spoke also a few words of -- of German language. I do not exactly know other kind of subjects, and I should have -- a subject more specifically. We also talked about, I remember, logistics, and heading of HBiH [sic] to Gornji Vakuf and maybe later to Prozor. Also was discussed the matter of harbour for the Muslims, south, these type of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And when you were discussing this issue of the harbour with the general, did he say anything else to you that may have stuck in your memory?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, let me first put one thing right. It was a meeting with UNPROFOR and two members of the ECMM, Peter Hauenstein and me, and we all put our questions. So if I specifically asked a specific question, I'm not sure but I heard the answers from this point of -- I got on with the answering of the question in specific to the field of the harbour. I do not know at this time how it ended. We also talked about Mostar and about the bridge in Mostar. General at that time has -- well, he was former director of theatre he told us, and he also made his gestures as a theatre man, broad, loud, and kind of friendly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can you remember what -- speaking about Mostar, can you remember what he may have said about the bridge in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. [Interpretation] Your Honour, it seems to me that the witness is reading a statement in responding, when he's answering, but can we clarify that? Is he reading his answers or not? And, if so, I'd like to have that on the record.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, when you answer the questions put to you, you have to look at the Prosecutor and to look at the Judges. Please do not read your written statement except if the Prosecutor wants you to read a specific portion of that statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not read my statement. The statement I know so far is from heart. I only looking to the monitor where I can see what the Prosecutor is saying and the other people in this room so I had -- I have a better understanding of what is told to me and asked to me. Anything else was by heart, but I will look into the room as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So, Colonel, going back to what you had mentioned you said, and I'll just remind you of it, we also talked about Mostar and the bridge in Mostar. Who --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Who was the one who brought up the issue of the bridge?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I do not know. The -- the general told us about destroying, for instance, Gornji Vakuf and also of destroying of the bridge of Mostar. It was -- and afterwards we had a discussion with UNPROFOR, Graham Binns, and with my colleague, Peter Hauenstein, because the words that were used I couldn't -- my English is not that well, but there were also -- were used more other words than only destroying and -- and that kind of discussions they conclude that it -- more serious days were coming. The general also told us that five minutes before shelling Gornji Vakuf UNPROFOR will be warned so we could take shelter. I must say, afterwards in my memory one time UNPROFOR was warned and the shelling in Gornji Vakuf was at the same amount as before.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Flynn, about the destruction of the Old Bridge in Mostar, you were told earlier on that this issue should not be raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I can't tell the accused what to say -- or the witness what to say, Your Honour. And this is all he has to say on the issue. And it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Flynn, if memory serves me right, the Mostar bridge was destroyed in November. Here we are talking about a meeting that took place on the 31st of July. Therefore, General Praljak can't be talking about the destruction of a bridge that's going to happen several months later. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really don't want to take up too much time, but my colleague said that the witness volunteered that. I'm reading page 33, line 1. He says: [In English] "So, Colonel, going back to what you had mentioned, you said, and I'll just remind you," leading, this is my comment, "I will just remind you of it. We also talked about Mostar and the bridge in Mostar."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's not the witness who put the question, but it is contained in the question. I didn't want to intervene. I knew that you would, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Please don't interrupt me, and read the transcript. I was reading the transcript word by word. [Interpretation] To continue, Your Honour, I want to protect my colleague in one portion because at the beginning when you gave your ruling, and that was on page 3, lines 13 to 16, when you gave your instructions there was a mistake in the transcript. You'll look at it later on. I'd like you to do so. But from the first part of your sentence there, it would appear as if you said that he was asking about the bridge, and it was only from the last part of the sentence, and something's missing there, is this portion, and you clarified that. "The questions will only talk about his written statement." So there was a mistake in the transcript and, therefore, a misunderstanding. So I don't hold it against my learned friend. But he cannot say that he did not expressly ask the witness about the bridge. And then you, Your Honour, told him not to ask the question. And it's all nonsensical if we look at the period of time involved. And this morning, when we were informed of this addition, no mention is made of the Old Bridge anywhere but of the Mostar bridge, and you, Your Honours, know that the -- there were some 12 or 14 bridges in Mostar. I never know whether it's 12 or 14. That's one point. And secondly, when the witness is speaking about this in context, he talks about the destruction in Gornji Vakuf, in Mostar, and he says, "the bridge." Which bridge? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thanks, Mr. Kovacic. Please proceed, Mr. Flynn.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I mean, if it's the instructions of the panel I'm not to talk about the bridge, I won't talk about the bridge. My next question would have been which bridge it was because he has never said which bridge. But I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: You mentioned that the -- the general spoke about Gornji Vakuf and the shelling of Gornji Vakuf; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can you remember anything specific what he may have said about that?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That -- that he has -- had the intention to destroy Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can you just turn to Exhibit 9638, please. Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: 31st of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Is that the daily report for the 31st of July?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, if you turn to paragraph 3, Military Activity.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And go halfway down the page -- halfway down the paragraph you'll see it says, "HVO appeared happy to level it," referring to Gornji Vakuf. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So what was your understanding when General Praljak made reference to this? Was it that he would not leave it standing?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, I didn't quite understand the word "to level." That's my problem with the English. It was for me destroy --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but -- thank you, Your Honour. I don't understand. I checked in the indictment, and there's no shelling as far as Gornji Vakuf is concerned in the indictment or what we're discussing now. So we don't have this overview, although it seems to relate to Gornji Vakuf. So I don't see where we're going. To seems we're going to discuss issues much broader than those contained in the indictment instead of reducing the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one brief point. Your Honour, this witness in the statement deals with Gornji Vakuf, and as I said, it's not indictment. Now, in addition to the statement the Prosecutor is asking him specific questions about that. These events in Gornji Vakuf, in the summer, are not part of the indictment. They are not contained in the indictment, because the situation is quite the opposite. It was the Croats that were attacked there by the BH army. That's why it's not in the indictment. But the essence of the matter is as follows: If the Prosecutor raises this question, then, Your Honour, we have a lot of evidence and very interesting material as far as Gornji Vakuf is concerned. So I propose that either the Prosecution ceases to put questions about Gornji Vakuf or we should be given additional time because we have a lot to say about Gornji Vakuf in order to put the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Flynn, if we look at the it indictment you will see that there's nothing about Gornji Vakuf. So what is your -- what is the purpose of your questions? What do you want to establish, except that General Praljak intended to level Gornji Vakuf? But even if that was established, in what way would that be of any assist tans to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: It shows the character of the gentleman who has a high position in the HVO. Now, I made it very clear at the outset to the witness that I was not going to dwell on issues related to Gornji Vakuf and Bugojno. But this in terms of the discussion with General Praljak showed the frame of mind -- shows the frame of mind General Praljak was in, shows his disposition to level a village or a town. Now, I'm not -- I'm not asking you solely to -- I would not be asking the panel solely to focus on Gornji Vakuf, but I believe I'm entitled to ask the question in the overall context of the meeting which took place because it demonstrates the general's disposition to destroy a town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but here again, Mr. Flynn, you know that in military terms, the warring factions have the right to attack a town if there are military objectives within that town. So if you're going along that avenue, you would have to ask more specific questions. The warring factions are entitled to attack a city or a town if the enemy has a stationed forces in that particular city or town. So if you want to deal with that particular issue, you would need to ask supplemental questions. You can't just ask that specific and limited question, even more so since you've noticed that the witness who is an English is not perfect has said that he had some duties about one word in that record. If I remember correctly, that was the word level. Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I, of course, completely agree with your instructions and guideline, yes, guidelines to the Prosecution, but my friend of the Prosecution mentioned another argument, that that was a position taken by one of the accused. I think that by saying that, this brings in subjectivism and, therefore, mens rea is called into question. But I'd like to follow on from that and say, of course questions have to be asked now and again for one to be able to conclude about mens rea. We all know that. We're all aware of that. But as far as I know through practice and what I was taught, the mens rea of an accused is always linked to actus reus, that is to say, a specific event, so that the accused at the time had such-and-such an opinion about something and then we can conclude and observe about mens rea. In this case we're talking about the 30th of July, 1993, and the place is Gornji Vakuf, and there's no indictment against my client or any of the accused in this courtroom as far as that is concerned. So even if there is a mens rea, it is once again irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We get the point. Mr. Flynn, please proceed and remember that what's important for the Judges is what's in the indictment, and when we come to subjective issues you have to be very careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: During the course of this meeting that you attended, do you remember if Colonel Siljeg actively participated in the discussion?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Most of the time not. It was more a monologue of General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And so at the conclusion of the meeting what was your opinion as to who was calling the shots in this area? Who was the overall commander?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, while the fighting was going on in Gornji Vakuf, were there preparations being made by the HVO to defend Prozor?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. We could witness that at Makljen check-point, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And if we turn very briefly to Exhibit 9657.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: The 2nd of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And do you -- is this a document which you authored?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And under General Situation, we have Prozor and Makljen check-point still remain in HVO hands. Under Military Activity as reported the BiH launched a full scale attack in the GV area last night. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So at this stage, was the ABiH moving southwards?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Was moving southwards, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Could -- now look at Exhibit 3909, please.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: The 3rd of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Again, is this the document which you participated in preparing?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And if we look under General Situation, the last sentence, it says, "Prozor remains actively with continued movement Makljen check-point is still in HVO hands and still is being prepared heavily for defence." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: If we turn to the humanitarian paragraph, do you see what's written there?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes I --

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: It says, "The GV BiH brigade commander stated that the only reason that they did not capture the Makljen check-point was that HVO used Muslim civilians as shields apparently. The HVO lined up 50 Muslim civilians between HVO positions and the attacking BiH." Is this something you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I'm familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Were you able to from your enquiries learn anything more than is contained there in the report about --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No. No. That was stated by ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you raise the issue with HVO authorities on or after that date the 3rd of August?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, these kind of questions we will always raised in the position with HVO commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you mention the matter to Colonel Siljeg?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Must be.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: But you cannot say for certain?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No. If there is no file, I'm -- I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Are you aware -- I just want to stay with this subject for a moment. Are you aware from any background information which you received on arrival or from what your colleagues may have told you if -- if ECMM had ever received similar information previous to your arrival concerning the use of forced labour like this?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I'm not -- I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So skipping forward a little for the moment after the 3rd of August, you say -- you said in your statement, your ICTY statement in the middle of page 9 of the English version that you had a meeting on the 19th of August with Commander Siljeg. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And if we turn to Exhibit 4307 --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: This is the 19th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And if you turn to the second page. When you met with Colonel Siljeg, what -- what was the subject of your discussion?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: We are permitted to visit the Muslim prisoners being held at the technical school in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Whether you say "Muslim prisoners," what type of prisoners were these?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: At a certain moment we have the opportunity to visit them. I don't know if this is the date, but -- this is not the date I presume, but at a certain moment we have visited these prisoners, and they appeared to be civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, we're talking about now the 19th of August, and in your report at page 2, is it stated that V2 was permitted to visit with 167 Muslim prisoners being held at the technical school in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And these prisoners, were they civilian prisoners or were they military prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: They were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And the report indicates that the men were between age 16 and 60, and it indicates that --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: -- you received some information that they were being used as forced labour by the HVO to dig trenches on the front lines in the Gornji Vakuf area.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: They told us so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And there was an allegation that some had died as a result of this work.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did they mention how many had died?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Oh, I do not know how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: After you had had the meeting with these -- these people, did you go back afterwards to express your concerns to Siljeg that there were people being used as forced labour on the front lines?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, we did several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And were you able at any stage to independently confirm the allegations of these individuals?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No. These type of questions we got the answer most of the times that they would investigate, and we got no results.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can you tell us at the time that you visit these prisoners who was actually guarding the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: As far as I can recall now, HVO members.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And these HVO, their commander was Colonel Siljeg?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, moving on in your ICTY statement at foot of page 10 in the English version you say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please wait a moment. I'd like to ask a point of clarification, because you mention the paragraph related to the visit to the prisoners. There's a sentence here, Colonel, that reads as follows in English: "[In English] We believe they are classed as civilian in terms under the Geneva Convention." [Interpretation] What allows you to write these words? On what basis can you write this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they were not military personnel, and, in terms of the Geneva Convention, civilians can't be POWs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, but according to you can civilians be detained as part of an administrative temporary procedure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when we asked for that, the -- these people were imprisoned for -- for their own safety, and these kind of answers we've got.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, are you then saying in this report that these are persons sheltered voluntarily rather than against their will?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying that. They were detained not on a voluntary basis. They were detained against their will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So you are not saying here that the detention is in conformity with the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not in conformity with the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I note that it's time for the break and I'm wondering if Your Honours wish to take the break at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Scott wants to take the floor first.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I apologise for delaying the break but hopefully it's best to resolve this now. I think I've learned in this trial perhaps more than any other about the importance of translation and what's sometimes in the transcript or not in the transcript. I'm not clear about the court's instruction in connection with the topic of the Old Bridge, and that's I think why Mr. Flynn and I both might be a both -- a bit at sea about this. Earlier today on page 3 of the transcript this is what came -- this is what is said on the transcript in English. I don't know if it's correct. I'm just simply reading what's on the face of the transcript. It says, "We learnt, and I thank the Prosecution, that they wanted to raise a topic with this witness, a topic that was not in the written statement of this witness, the destruction of the Old Bridge in Mostar, and the Judges that evoked this question deem that this is a topic that's interesting to raise through this witness." And so I certainly heard that at the time it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a mistake. We never said that it was a question that would be interesting to -- to discuss. We said that, according to the Judges, this matter should not be raised. It's precisely the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then at least I hope the Trial Chamber will understand our confusion because I read exactly from the transcript what we heard. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My attention had been drawn to that fact, but for me it was so straightforward that I did not believe that it was necessary for me to correct this thing. But you're absolutely right. I should have then corrected that sentence in English. We have a translation problem here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I completely agree with you. I also warned that the sentence was not clear and that's why my colleague referred back to the transcript. But the colleague -- my colleague did quote part of that incorrectly, written sentence, but failed to quote the last part of the sentence, and we saw that something was amiss and wrong but I didn't know what it was. So, when it comes to a quotation one should always have the sense to read the whole sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We'll have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Before proceeding, I would like to hand the floor to the registrar because he wishes to give us a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I've received a list submitted by 6D in relation to the documents they want to tender with Witness Philip Watkins, and that list shall be given Exhibit number IC 586, Your Honours.
