utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So a term that has taken a meaning all of its own as a result of the civil war that occurred in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But it would be fair to say that if civilians picked up and left because they were in the middle of a fighting area, would you call that ethnic cleansing or would you call that perhaps good old common sense: Get out of the way?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. In a fighting situation, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And you as a monitor there were not able to assess them because, first, you weren't there to do that; right?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were there to simply monitor?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And even if you wanted to, you didn't have the capabilities?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No materiel and personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, Uzdol, as I understand it you went there?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You went there after the incident?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You and I believe it was the --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: The 15th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And you were, in fact, invited by the mayor of Prozor.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Jozic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you able to conduct -- I don't want to say investigation because that has sort of a real technical definition or perception, you know, but you wanted to see what happened; right?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you find the mayor?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did he talk to you?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was he open?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did he want to share with you what had happened to the Croats at Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. It was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Because But after all, he had invited you, right?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. That was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. No problem -- did you by any chance want to see any of those people that had left Uzdol, assuming that any one of them, you know, had survived?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I have seen only dead people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And when you saw the dead people, did you see them in situ, where they actually had been killed or --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: A few of them, and some in Prozor and -- the most of them were already gathered in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: And some of them were still in Uzdol.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you've been in battle before. You're military trained. You were there to observe. Do you think, do you think by any chance they might have transported dead bodies and put them there to make it look like it had happened, or were you convinced, based on your knowledge, experience, and having witnessed what -- what had indeed happened, were you convinced that indeed that situation occurred as it was described to you or as you saw it?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] In other words.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That specific situation Uzdol, I don't think it was all set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That -- that's not my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you have -- with you were -- was a reporter or some journalists?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, Kate Adie. Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I can't recall the name.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, Kate Adie.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I know they were there and I know they were there when you were there, and I take it since you were there at the behest of the mayor they were -- they also allowed the journalists to have a walkabout, take photographs, videotape, do interviews.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- I might -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Perhaps you're leading somewhere. I just can't see it, but what --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You weren't here last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: What's sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander, and given that I have not -- I have kept away specifically from Bugojno and Gornji Vakuf, because it does not form part of the indictment. To my knowledge, Uzdol doesn't form part of the indictment either. Perhaps you have a point to make but I'm just wondering when you'll get to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll just make it very briefly, Your Honour. We had one particular witness - I don't wish to name the witness, but he was in closed session - indicated that a few days later went there. The mayor would not cooperate. The mayor wasn't going to do anything. Was unable to confirm anything. Indeed, his report ended going up even further up the chain and being reported in essence nothing had happened in Uzdol, and here we have somebody there at the behest of the same individual who had invited this other person, was able to see it, is confirming it, which goes to perhaps why the Croats at times thought that one particular organisation may have been less than balanced in their reporting. So I think -- and my learned friend wasn't here at the time, but I think the Trial Chamber knows exactly what I'm talking about. If not, I can deal with that -- I'm told the initials are Witness BC. So -- and I thought that this was well within the range of topics because Uzdol was mentioned earlier. So -- but I'll move on. That's all I needed for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I don't have much time, that's why I'm covering a lot of ground. I don't mean to be rude.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No, no, you are not. You are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, you said in one of your -- in one of your statements, and I sort of thought about this, it sort of caught my attention, that the Muslims played their cards well.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In fact, you went on to say they were playing the media well as well.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're saying mm-hmm; that means yes?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that means yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I take it that you're giving to give us some fuller explanation of that because I think I know what you mean. But could you kind of tell us in your own words what do you mean by they played the media and they played their cards well? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, I think it was one of their aims to get -- to do it well in the international community. For instance, we always ask why in Gornji Vakuf the civilian people from the Croats were left -- were not left, were gone, were evacuated, and the Muslim civilian people stayed in Gornji Vakuf, and I think it was possible to evacuate these people as well. And there was a war going on, and Gornji Vakuf was shelled on a daily basis. These kind of facts gives me that meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The impression.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: The impression, yes. And opposite the Croats, well, they made the same mistakes. That's obvious for me. But I think you spoke about me to be naive. Well, one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: One way or another, well, I think it's my opinion that the Croats were also a bit naive in -- in not the right way but prepare the international community, the -- to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me help you out here.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In other words --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: My English is not that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But I think we're on the same wavelength. In other words, I think what you're trying to tell the Trial Chamber is that on the public relations front?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: On the -- yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The Muslims were able to play the media?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And play the internationals like a violin?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Okay. That's right. That's very beautiful, a violin, but okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: They were able -- and when you say naivete, you say when you scratch the surface, at least when you initially went there you might be led into believing whatever you were told by them, but the longer you were there the more you were able to see --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- some of the games that they were playing; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You also indicated that the -- at least in Bugojno the Muslim army was much more organised or better organised than the Croat, the HVO. We have to make a record so you have to say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Hmm, hmm. It's difficult to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm just going by what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Because a losing army -- is not a total army in Bugojno, just a brigade, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: But a losing brigade is always not well-organised, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: They're retreating.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Because they're retreating.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Losing ground.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: So it's difficult to answer. But at that time it was my opinion that the Muslim army was better organised, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that you also said that they -- that they were -- that they were more sophisticated than the HVO.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, only the people I talked to. As a -- a sum --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Okay. Now, I want to go back a little bit to what we were talking about earlier, the public relations game, and then also perhaps using -- using civilians as part of their cards. You indicated earlier that the -- that the civilians in Gornji Vakuf, that they were kept there. The Muslim civilians. You're shaking your head. That means yes.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That means yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand you, and correct me if I'm wrong - I don't want to put any words in your mouth - that it was your understanding that they were being kept there by the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: They were not allowed to go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: To leave. Okay. Well --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Just my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's what we're talking about. You're here to share your opinion. You were there. I wasn't. The Trial Chamber wasn't. But one could conclude, in other words, that it was the ABiH that was preventing them from leaving because earlier we said that if you're in the middle of a war zone --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- and if you have any sense you're going to get out of there?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then they were being kept there against their will by the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I notice one other thing. I've got to slow down a little bit because we're tiring the interpreters out.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I am, not you. So let me take a pause, let them catch up. In reading your statements and reading your testimony, I also got the impression that the Muslim army, the ABiH, was sort of inviting or trying to cajole, if you would, the Croat civilians to stay in various pockets. Am I correct in that? Did I draw the right conclusion?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I must read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Was sort of finding or trying --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: To cajole, to keep them, to keep the Croats in certain villages?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: What's the meaning of "cajole"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Were trying to convince them to stay.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Okay. Trying to convince them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So there would be pockets of Croats?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Oh, they did in Bugojno. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay. And, I take it, this way, as far as the public relations front would be for those of us who might have been naive in reading the papers, see, the Muslim intention coming out of Sarajevo is they are trying to protect the Croatian people and maintain the status quo, unlike the Serbs or the Croats. That would be one.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're -- okay. The other one, however, and I thought that I gleaned this from -- from what you were trying to say and might have even said it, that the other reason would have been that by keeping the Croats there in these pockets the -- they would need supplies.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Ah. And then --

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: It's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: But a logical one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: A logical one. And one that you drew from being there; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Karnavas, I'm sorry. It seems to me that this was not covered by direct, so I think you should not ask leading questions all the time as you do. Wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree with you, Your Honour. I think -- I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's your duty, but nevertheless I think I'm right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I Well, don't think you're right here. The gentleman was there. I'm asking him about his impressions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. Let me make my record and you can reprimand me all you want, but he was allowed to testify about his impressions in the field. That's a wide -- that's a wide area. One of the impressions was what the intentions were of the parties. The Prosecution on numerous occasions asked him what he perceived, what he believed, what he thought the intentions were, and my question is: Why should we be afraid of this kind of testimony? Am I not here to get the truth to you? I'm trying. Now, I can bring the gentleman back on direct examination, but I don't see how else I can lead him into this area and then ask him to explain to us what he thought, what he saw, what he believed, what his impressions were, because the Prosecution did that. It's the same period of time, same location, same everything. He was -- so he was asking what the Croats -- I'm asking what the Muslims. Same thing. I don't -- I really don't see it. I'm not trying to be argumentative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You have just said, Mr. Karnavas, you could bring him back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But I have to lead. I have to get it -- I have to get it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Exactly, and I'm not saying you can't ask him what you're asking him. But I think you should ask him as if you had brought him in direct, and that is to say by not putting leading question after leading question. That's all. And that's what the Chamber has recently ruled and I think you should abide by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand what they have ruled. I thought I was in the same area. If I have transgressed, I apologise. I'll try. Do keep in mind, Your Honour, that I haven't prepped -- proofed the witness, so he may need -- and I have limited time. That's the other problem. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Flynn.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Flynn.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: If I may make one comment, Your Honours. I had kept my powder dry, and I was watching Mr. Karnavas's examination of the witness. And it appeared to me that most of his questions were directed to what his impressions were, what intentions were -- there were relative to Bugojno and to Gornji Vakuf. Now, I purposely kept away from those areas because they weren't part of the indictment, and I feel that the same criteria should apply to Mr. Karnavas. It wasn't part of the evidence, and his cross-examination should focus on the direct -- the direct -- the examination-in-chief and keep away from the areas in which we're not talking about. I don't see that it's advancing the case one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Whose case is? I'm advancing my own. I'm not here to advance the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Very well. I'm quite happy if you waste your time, but I just don't see it advancing the case. And we're here to save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, a small reminder. At the beginning of the afternoon you were not present. We found out through the Prosecutor, who had sent e-mails, that he had the intention to put questions about the Old Bridge. The Chamber deliberated and told Mr. Flynn that he should not ask questions on this topic, and then a debate took place in your absence, and the Defence counsel represented by Mr. Kovacic, he raised questions about Bugojno and Gornji Vakuf and stated that even -- that those two places were not in the indictment and this is why the Prosecution should not ask questions regarding those two places. So the Defence deemed that that was what should take place, but you're doing exactly the contrary of what Mr. Kovacic requested. You are now asking -- you're starting a subject that your own colleague did not want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may -- if I may respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Granted I wasn't here, and I abide by whatever decisions were made prior to my arrival. However, what I am questioning the witness about, about his impressions, go well beyond, well beyond this limited area. What I'm trying to suggest to the Trial Chamber, that here for the first time we have a gentleman who is able to provide us with impressions of what the Muslims were trying to achieve, and if they were trying to achieve it in this particular area, does it not stand to logic that they were also applying that to other air? In other areas they're trying to win the public relations game. In other areas they're using their own people as hostages, in a sense. In other areas they're trying to pretend that they really are concerned about the Croats when they really want to use them for the public relations, and also because they will need to be supplied and they can squeeze and turn off the circuit any time they wish. So this is what I'm trying to show, that there is a wider gain. Now, if I have gone into an area that perhaps my brethren did not want to go into due to the lack of time, it wasn't my intention to go into the specifics but merely to draw from this gentleman the knowledge that he has obtained from the field, from observing as a career officer what his intentions and impressions were, because after all I listened very carefully for the little time that I was here, and I did think that my learned friend on the Prosecution side also asked for impressions. Now, if I'm wrong, I'll sit down. I was nearly completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So please proceed and complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. And I apologise to Judge Trechsel for my exuberance earlier. I understand the ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes. You do that often. You raise your voice very often, Mr. Karnavas, and if you can cut it down a bit and not shout down the Judges, then it is a bit better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I don't wish to debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, sir, going back to where we were. The Muslims were also trying to convince the Croats to stay in pockets because that way they could also control the supply lines; right?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Explain that a little bit. I don't want to lead you, but give us a fuller explanation. I think I may have another minute or two.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, it's more -- well, if you have a minority of people, it's obvious that all kind of humanitarian aid is coming in. In the example of Bugojno, aid was brought in for the Croat minority, which was sold out by the mayor of Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Say that again. I didn't hear you. Say that again. Aid was coming in for the Croats and then the mayor -- and he was a Croat as well?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No. The mayor in Bugojno was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Ah, I see. So aid would come in for the Croats and then the Muslims would use -- would sell the aid. So this is one way, at least you could use Croats, to get good supplies.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Just an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's just an example.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, I want to thank you -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: These things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: These things happened. Right. But in that example, and other examples as well, is what allow you to form the impressions that you shared with us; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So in other words, you're not speculating, you're watching. You're seeing. You're seeing all of these events; right?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: This was my job in the ECMM, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. Sir, I want to thank you for coming here and clarifying some matters, and good luck in your career.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's it for my cross-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have handed out the documents that I'm going to use. I have given them to the registrar and he will distribute them, one for the witness, and one for yourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. We will go into my documents later on, so you don't have to look at the binder straight away. Now, with respect to the questions my learned friend asked you a moment ago and with respect to the objections made by the Prosecution about the situation of Croats in Bugojno, and in view of the fact that events were taking place at the same time in Bugojno as they were Prozor, and you said that quite certainly one set of events was reflected on the other set of events. Would you take a look at document P 0 -- in the Prosecutor's binder, that is, P 0 -- that's the Prosecutor binder. So the other one.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Oh, the other one. Okay. The Prosecutor's.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: P 09629 is the number of the document I'd like you to look at. Tell me when you find it, please. 9629.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: The daily report of the 13th of September?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That's right. And I'd like to look at the 13th of September, 1993, with respect to the situation of the Croats in Bugojno. Number 2, paragraph 2, the Political Situation. I'm going to read it out slowly because it says here that "V2," which is yourself, is that right? That's you, "met with the Bugojno HDZ leadership today and were briefed on the party's political platform. Their platform is as follows: They want normalisation of the community relations with the Muslims --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry Ms. Nozica. The president has recalled a short while ago that this morning the Defence led by Mr. Kovacic -- early afternoon, sorry -- made it quite clear that it would not be correct to put questions on Bugojno because that was not covered by the indictment. And I'm amazed that you start off right away asking questions about Bugojno. I find that a bit contradictory, I must say. Not quite fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I might be allowed to say something. A moment ago the Presiding Judge, Judge Antonetti, said the same thing. However, the fact is that my objection was overruled, and the fact is that the Prosecution did proceed to question the witness about Bugojno and Gornji Vakuf, and I intervened twice. I was on my feet twice and reminded the Trial Chamber that if this can have any relevance bearing in mind that entire area that we were thereby opening up an area that the Defence will have to examine on later on, and I can find it in the transcript if you want to, but my objection was to Gornji Vakuf, first and foremost, because it was the time that was -- a period of time that wasn't relevant and went in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I be allowed to add something? What Mr. Kovacic said, however the Trial Chamber understands it, was not stated on behalf of all the Defence teams. I consider, and the witness said so himself, that these two events, the one in Bugojno and in Prozor, are closely related. Now, you say that you're surprised. I am showing a document that the Prosecution presented and showed to the witness during the examination-in-chief. That's what I'm referring to. But I'm just referring to other portions of the document, because I consider that it is impossible to view the situation in Prozor isolated from other events if we don't know what went on before and later on in that overall area. And this document was highlighted to confirm what the witness answered in response to a question from my learned friend Mr. Karnavas, because what impressions the witness gave is what is in fact written down in this report. So with your permission, I'd like to carry on with the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to tell you that I was also much surprised in seeing all the material on Bugojno in the statement presented by the -- by the Prosecutor. So this is not unilateral. Don't think that I did not notice in the first place that there was a slightly strange situation with this witness. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, may we carry on discussing the document? Have you had a chance to have a look at it? "The HDZ of Bugojno is trying to stay in Bugojno. They want to have a normalised relations with the Muslims. They say that they recognise the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that they want the Croat operation of Bugojno to return to the city." It says: "The main aim of the HDZ is to save Croat lives," and therefore they understand the need to maintain good relationships with the civil war Presidency authority. The city's government has made a number of promises to the Croat minority and then they say that they're sending a message to the Croats in Prozor, not to undertake any drastic action because that could reflect on them. Now, there's a comment of yours, I assume, here, which says the civilian and military authorities of Prozor do not support the reintegration the Croatian minority in Bugojno. They ask, "Where will they live? All the houses have all been burnt. Reintegration is only an empty phrase. Other reasons are More obvious like the use of the Croat minority as hostages to secure humanitarian aid." Again the same authorities express the need for more information on the Jablanica-Konjic areas as they have little access to sources, et cetera, et cetera. So am I right in saying that your answer, and we'll deal with this document some more later on, but your answer, the answer you gave to Mr. Karnavas about the desires of the authorities in Bugojno to have the Croats stay on, not to have them reintegrated in their society, is exact, and that is how it is expressed in your report.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Well, that is correct. It's still the same after all these years.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us now take a look at paragraph 4 of the report relating to humanitarian activity. Paragraph 4. And I'm using this document to draw a parallel to what is happening in Prozor. This is the 13th of September. The penultimate observation in point 4 states: "The Croat minority in Bugojno reports that there are 50 Croats, POWs, living in the mosque at Gornji Vakuf." And shall we look at paragraph 8, Military Assessment. "No change on the military assessment from our previous report," it says. The situation in Bugojno for the Croatian minority is still deteriorating despite the so-called promises of -- made by the local Muslim authorities. V2 expects this trend to continue." Now, sir, I've shown you this document because it fully reflects what your answers said in response to Mr. Karnavas's questions about the politics and policies of the authorities in Bugojno towards the Croatian minority which stayed on there. Can you confirm that based on this document?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask you - once again in the Prosecution binder - to draw a parallel and take a look at the next document, P 09661. Tell me when you've found it, please.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I have found the daily report of the 9th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Now let's take a look at paragraph 4. This was a document shown to you by the Prosecutor, but they focused on another part of the document. I'd like to look at your observations about prisoners of war in Prozor. And in the third or second -- second or third sentence it says: "Looking at it overall, the conduct towards the prisoners is good. They have enough water and food, and it seems that their living conditions appear to be fairly reasonable. They have the possibility for adequate washing and sanitary facilities. V2 pick up some mail from the detainees and will deliver it as required. The local authorities promised to provide you," that is a the members of the V2 team, "with a list of all POWs and the remaining Muslims in the area." And we have an addition where it says: "The visits -- the V2's visit included a visit to two factories where about 40 prisoners live and work. The living conditions there are very good, and the internees are -- have limited free access to the city." All I wanted to do and what I'm doing is to confirm that where the prisoners were held, that the conditions were as you have described them here. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like briefly to go to another area, and P 9654, P 09654, is once again a Prosecution document, and it refers to this next area that I'd like to deal with. Tell me when you've found it. P 09654. Shall we take a look at paragraph 3 together now. And it relates to an important activity of yours, and a number of reports deal with it, some shown to you by the Prosecutor, others not, with respect to moving the wounded from Bugojno. And this report is dated the 21st of July, 1993. And paragraph 2 of section 3 describes the situation, and it says: "Doctors from the French organisation there say that they expect that at least 20 persons will die during the night because they have no water, no electricity, and no food." Can you tell me to the best of your recollections, and we'll take a look at other documents as well, how far you remember this situation and what you can tell us about this dramatic appeal from this report? Anything else you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes. This is -- these are people in the HVO war hospital in the Hotel Kalin, and we witnessed that. "We" is the ECMM and UNPROFOR at that time. And the situation was there as described. It's also in our own reports from Victor 2, and that was the situation up there, yes. You asked for my own words. Well, it was a terrible situation. There were there people, wounded people, no electricity, no fuel, and they try -- there was still a doctor and nurse, and they tried to operate and so on and so on, and it wasn't possible. So at the end of this story, it's quite a story, it's -- we evacuated the hospital from Hotel Kalin.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. You referred to that in a number of reports. V2, yes. The Prosecutor didn't use those reports of yours. But now if you refer to my binder. And you were a participant in that evacuation. 2D 00461 is the document I'd like to refer to in my binder. Tell me if you've found it.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. This is a final appeal to save the wounded from Bugojno, signed by the commander. Colonel Zeljko Siljeg is the signatory. And for the HVO Medical Corps, Dr. Ivo Sandrk signed. And this final appeal was sent to BritBat, Major Binns whom you mentioned, UN British Battalion, Major Binns, and to Captain Holden. This is a very dramatic appeal. I'm just going to ask you whether what he says is exact. He says: "I am addressing you maybe for the last time so that we together try to do everything to save the lives of hundreds of wounded children, civilians, Croatian soldiers from Bugojno. Already tomorrow such help may not be needed. Many of them died due to most simple wounds, and many are still lying in the streets and in front of burnt down homes. Together we were witnesses to the horrors at the war hospital of Bugojno (ex-Hotel Kalin). We saw only motionless human beings as they are slowly dying because no medical assistance could be rendered to them. There is no water, electricity," et cetera. Now, take a look at this next sentence: "Together with the wounded members of the HVO there are also as helpless 12 members of Muslim armed forces." The MOS. Do you know the abbreviation M-O-S and what M-O-S is -- stands for?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: No. Military off the shelf, but that's something different.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: No. It is the Muslim armed forces.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: M-O-S, Muslim armed forces. Now we come to the essential portion. "I am asking of you to influence Muslim armed forces command to help and save them as well. You saw at the MOS war hospital, where there is about 150 wounded, that they have everything." And then it goes on to say: "To no wounded Croatian child, civilian or soldiers, from the beginning no medical assistance or almost no medical assistance could be rendered," et cetera. Have you heard of this appeal and can you confirm what it says here? Was that the situation that people really found themselves at that period?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I -- this is the first time I see this appeal, and I -- I think it's correct also. In my point of view it's a bit exaggerated because -- but then I have to study to it. Hundred and fifty wounded, I do not know of them. I think there were a lot of people. A hundred and fifty wounded, but I am confused by the wounded in Kalin hotel. There was -- there were also wounded people in the hospital of the ABiH, which -- which was held by the ABiH in Bugojno. So it's a bit confusing for me. I -- because I do not know this, but I think it's -- it's correct. It's correct. But, it's a way of saying I'm not used to. You understand? We were more -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do understand. You and I both understand that the doctor who was responsible for their lives in such a dramatic moment, which was confirmed by the French non-governmental medical organisation, has the right to use a more dramatic tone, but I'd just like to remind you that these 150 wounded does not refer to the Croatian wounded who were to be evacuated, but it says here, "You saw at the MOS war hospital where there is about 150 wounded." So these 150 wounded -- yes. Just to deal with that dilemma so as to not create problems in the future. Now, I'm going to show you another document, and it reflects the same situation more or less. I don't have much time so I can't go through all the documents, but take a look at the next document, 2D 00466, just to show you that it was an objective representation of the situation and not an exaggeration. There's a document here which -- well, it's the same date, the 21st of July, signed by same person, and he says what the situation is like in the hospital. And he says that there are 13 seriously wounded HVO members, 12 wounded MOS men, and 150 civilians who fled the settlement of Gaj. "There is no water or electricity, and for two days already there is no food. The wounded did not have their bandages renewed for two days because --" et cetera. "Access to the hospital is impossible due to the snipers and tank. I have information that we had quite a number of wounded that have not been taken care of in Vucipolje," et cetera. "The brigade commander at Bugojno has issued an appeal for help in manpower." Is that the situation as you remember it?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Now, I don't want to burden you any more with this, but I'd just like to remind you that on the 29th of July, 1993, or thereabouts with your assistance and the assistance of your team and UNPROFOR, these persons were indeed evacuated can we confirm?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to ask you about another evacuation operation that was mentioned in this courtroom, and I'll just ask you whether you recall it. Do you remember the evacuation of a young girl, she was a Muslim young girl, and she was evacuated to Split and she suffered from leukaemia. And let me remind you if you don't know anything about that, that that was an intervention from General Praljak. He intervened that she should be evacuated. Do you remember that event?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask you to look at the document addressing the matter together. 2D 00464 is the number. Tell me when you've found it.

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The date is the 11th of September, 1993, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Right. The document is from the medical sector, Mostar defence, and it is signed by Dr. Pero Maric. Now, let's see whether this is the case he addresses. He says, "On the 11th of September, 1993, pursuant to an order from the head of the control and inspection service attached to the sector for health, Dr. Ivo Sandrk, and pursuant to an order from General Praljak, I was an escort as a doctor to the sick child leukaemia in remission by the maim of Haris Silajdzija, who is four and a half years old, and his mother Enisa, his younger brother who is two years old, on the locality of the war hospital Rama at Rumboci to Split. The mother and children were transported from Bugojno by UNPROFOR and the European observers." As far as I can see, your name is mentioned there as well. "And we set out for Split at 1430 hours and arrived at 1800 hours. At the Firule hospital in Split they were taken over by Dr. Skrabic."

utterances.speaker: RUDY GERRITSEN
utterances.text: Yes, and my registration number is not correct. The last three should be 155, but it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. We have now corrected this. That's very significant. Sir, my time is running out, so I will move on to one last topic,.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But may we move into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're back in open session. Colonel, you were under oath, meaning that you are a witness of the Court, of the justice. You are not a Prosecutor's witness, meaning that you will no longer have any contacts with the Prosecutor. You will be back here for the hearing that will start at 2.15 p.m. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 30th day of May, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.04 p.m.,
